auditor_rubric_notes:
WHERE I DREW THE HARD BOUNDARY (narration vs own-claim change). I asked, for every row: does THIS hunt's own recorded text stop saying what it said? Rows 3 and 9 both cite another hunt's kill report or another hunt's withdrawal, and I still marked them revisions, because in both cases the sentence that changed is this hunt's own (wide_search's HANDOFF withdrew its own 0.6725124 candidate; outband_certificate rewrote its own title, verdict and grade). Row 24 is the mirror image: it reports that a control battery fired and that another party's disagreement stands, but every existing sentence in the file survives unchanged, so it is narration plus new work, not revision. Row 20's fix (the BandCert import defect) was landed in the hunt's own Lean package, so the narration boundary does not exclude it; I still called it no, on the separate rule below.

A SECOND LINE I HAD TO DRAW, AND IT DECIDED FIVE ROWS. The rubric's "a number that changed" and "a statement replaced by a contradicting one" will fire on any hunt that says "X is missing / X does not build / the bridge stops at 0.5" and later does the work. I separated: (a) a recorded claim that was WRONG WHEN WRITTEN, or a number replaced because the earlier one was in error, or an explicit withdrawal/retraction/narrowing = revision (rows 2, 3, 7, 9, 10, 12, 14, 17, 19, 21, 23, 26); (b) a recorded STATE that changed because the hunt did the work it had itself named as the next step = not a revision (rows 16, 20, 28). Checks that fixed (b): BANDWIDTH-FORENSICS section 11 had already classed the half-band stop as "a proof-technology barrier" and listed the long-polynomial mean-value route that row 16 then takes; O9-LEAF-REPAIR named rIv, qreIv, sqrScaled as the missing definitions that row 28 writes; the zeta23ext README's pin-note correction predates row 20's commit. Row 14 is on the other side of that line despite also being an instrument upgrade, because the hole map moved in BOTH directions (nu = 1.45 flips from hole to closed, 1.1 and 1.2 flip into the hole), so the earlier map was wrong, not merely loose.

THREE ROWS CANNOT BE JUDGED FROM THEIR OWN TEXT (4, 22, 29): files_touched empty, diff empty. I answered no for all three, on the ground that a row with no claim-file change carries no revision. Row 4 is the sharp one and is a sampling artifact worth reporting: it is a merge, and reading the repository shows its second parent brings a paragraph headed "Historical progression, now withdrawn" into hunts/frontier_math/RESULTS-frontier-math.md. That text was authored by commit 58ddf4c on the merged branch, so scoring the merge as a revision would count one withdrawal twice, and scoring it from the row as given is impossible in either direction.

Distribution: 13 revisions, 17 not. The revision set is dominated by explicit self-labelled defects (#10, #18, #19/#20), two outright withdrawals, one refuted Lean table, and one decimal-tail correction.
auditor_expected_disagreements:
Ranked by how likely I am to differ from the repaired classifier.

1. ROW 8 (lexical-gate fix), my weakest label. I said revision because the commit repairs previously committed ledger text and records it as "session defect #10". A classifier tuned to claim content will say no, since the mathematics, the sorry count and the disclosure all stand and only a reserved word was reworded, which is typo-adjacent. I would not defend my label hard; what I would defend is that the row needs an explicit rule, because "a defect in the hunt's own earlier work being fixed" and "a typo / formatting sweep" both cover it and the rubric does not say which wins.

2. ROW 20 (zeta23ext README). The commit subject contains the word "contradicted", and three paragraphs are rewritten from present to past tense with a defect marked "now FIXED". A literal reader of "a statement replaced by a contradicting one" says yes; I said no under the state-of-work rule. If the classifier keys on subject lines this row will disagree, and it is the row where a keyword-driven classifier and a content-driven one part company most cleanly.

3. ROW 16 (crossing the half-band). Same shape as row 20 but with a mathematical barrier instead of a build status, and the new document says "the old gamma<delta condition was a worst-spacing loss", which reads as declaring an earlier constraint an artifact. I checked the predecessor commit before deciding: the hunt had already written that the obstruction was proof-technology and named this exact way out, so I called it continuation. Reasonable people land the other way.

4. ROW 5 (resummed bridge). Almost entirely new material, but it does fix a citation (Farmer-Gonek to Farmer-Gonek-Lee) and weaken one goal word (rigorous to exact). If the classifier treats any in-place correction of a recorded fact as a revision, it says yes.

5. ROW 7 (prime_pair_error third pass). The headline is a large addition, and the revision lives in five small in-place hedges, chiefly "E(N) is noise" becoming "most of E(N) remains unexplained by the tested corrections". A classifier reading the commit subject or the added section will call this pure extension and miss the retraction; a diff-level reader should catch it.

6. ROW 24 (gate #3 fires) and ROW 15 (k>=2 anatomy). Both contain strong-sounding refutation language ("kill condition fires", "void, not a finding", "a disagreement left standing", "Incidence is not limited") aimed at things other than the hunt's own recorded claims. These are the two rows most likely to produce a false positive in a classifier that scores vocabulary rather than target.

7. ROW 4 (merge). Disagreement here is about corpus construction, not about the commit: any answer is defensible when the row carries no diff, and the underlying withdrawal is already attributable to another commit.
